name: Profhilo / skin booster injectables

lead: Profhilo and similar skin boosters are injected to make skin look more hydrated, supple and smooth, improving skin quality rather than adding volume the way a filler does. They are often positioned as a complement to fillers.

Profhilo, made by IBSA and sold in Europe since 2015, combines high and low molecular weight hyaluronic acid, which is proposed to hydrate the dermis and stimulate fibroblasts to make collagen and elastin. Small open-label studies and post-marketing data report gains in hydration and elasticity.

paras: It is injected into the skin by a clinician, in a short series of sessions. The skin-booster category covers products placed in the dermis for hydration, elasticity and texture. Many people combine it with filler or other skin treatments.

Reported effects are mostly minor swelling, redness and bruising. Hyaluronic acid injectables can rarely cause vascular occlusion. One source states Profhilo was not FDA-approved in the US as of January 2026.

angle.text: Profhilo and similar skin boosters are used to give a more hydrated, supple and smoother-looking complexion rather than added volume. Hyaluronic acid injected into the skin helps it hold more water, improving hydration and elasticity. Small studies report these gains.

lead: Profhilo is an injectable hyaluronic acid (HA) product made by IBSA Derma, the aesthetics division of the Swiss pharmaceutical company IBSA, and launched in Europe in 2015. It is marketed as a skin 'bio-remodelling' treatment rather than a volume filler. Each syringe combines high and low molecular weight HA stabilised by a heat process, with no chemical cross-linker.[1]

The way it is meant to improve looks is through skin quality: smoother, better-hydrated, firmer-looking skin on the face, neck, hands and body, rather than the added bulk of a cheek or lip filler. Practitioners describe the chain as hydration and tissue remodelling, then improved elasticity and texture, then a fresher, less crepey appearance. It is typically given as a short course of sessions about a month apart, followed by maintenance.[1][2]

Profhilo belongs to a broader category called skin boosters: injectables placed in the dermis to improve hydration, elasticity and texture instead of adding volume, which also includes other HA products, polynucleotides and further materials. A 2024 review in Archives of Plastic Surgery describes the main types of skin boosters, how they work and the evidence for them in aging skin.[3]

Published evidence includes small open-label studies, randomised split-face trials, a 2026 systematic review of nine studies and ten years of post-marketing safety surveillance, much of it with manufacturer involvement.[4][5][6] As of January 2026, one source states that Profhilo was not FDA-approved in the US, while it carries CE marking in Europe.[1]

paras: Each 2 ml syringe is reported to hold 64 mg of HA, half high molecular weight (about 1,100 to 1,400 kDa) and half low (about 80 to 100 kDa), produced by bacterial fermentation and combined by IBSA's patented NAHYCO (hybrid cooperative complex) process with heat rather than chemical cross-linking.[1] Proponents describe 'hybrid cooperative complexes' that they say are more resistant to enzymatic breakdown and activate cellular processes in skin. A 2016 laboratory paper in PLoS One reported that the complexes raised collagen and elastin gene expression in cultured skin cells more than either HA component alone; the journal issued an expression of concern about that paper in April 2024.[7]

The product is used on the face, neck and body. Because the gel is described as spreading through tissue rather than holding a shape, it is positioned against cross-linked fillers that restore volume and contour.[1]
Skin boosters as a class include HA, polynucleotides and other materials, and reviews discuss their types and mechanisms.[3]

IBSA (Institut Biochimique SA) is a Swiss company founded in Lugano in 1945 by Swiss biologists, and its IBSA Derma division focuses on aesthetics. Profhilo, the first product built on its NAHYCO technology, launched in Europe in 2015 with CE marking.[1]

Post-marketing safety assessments followed in 2020 and 2025. In China, an exclusive distribution agreement with Sisram Medical was announced in 2023, and in the UK and Ireland IBSA moved to direct distribution in 2026, according to one reference page that itself carries a note about internal inconsistencies, so dates and counts should be read as approximate.[1]

Profhilo is used on the face, neck, chest, hands and body to address skin laxity, roughness and fine wrinkles, and is often grouped with other skin boosters.[1][8] A 2025 review of non-facial rejuvenation of the neck, chest and hands covers injectable options including this kind of product.[8]

Practitioners combine it with other treatments. A randomised trial in neck rejuvenation compared botulinum toxin alone with botulinum toxin followed by Profhilo gel,[9] and a split-face randomised trial added Profhilo mesogel to subcision for atrophic acne scars.[10]

Profhilo Body is a variant for the body, and Profhilo Structura is a higher-concentration formulation with 45 mg of total hyaluronic acid developed to restore facial adipose tissue, with a practical review focused on the superficial medial and lateral-temporal cheek fat compartments.[11] An initial case series in 22 volunteers aged 36 to 60 used Profhilo Structura in superficial fat of each hemiface.[12]

Profhilo is delivered as small intradermal and superficial injections rather than deep depot placement. One reference page describes a standard facial course of two sessions about 30 days apart, followed by maintenance sessions at intervals of around two months, with each visit lasting roughly 15 to 30 minutes and performed by a licensed practitioner.[1] The same source describes a small number of injection points on each side of the face, placed with fine needles according to a mapped pattern, and notes that topical anaesthetic is optional. IBSA names its placement pattern the Bio-Aesthetic Points technique.[1]

Because the gel is spread by the tissue rather than moulded into shape, practitioners describe the visible result as gradual skin change rather than an immediate contour change. A 2018 expert panel on stabilised non-animal HA skin boosters described a standard initial protocol of up to three sessions followed by maintenance treatments, with texture continuing to improve for up to 12 months when repeated every 4 to 6 months.[2]

Reported after-effects are redness, swelling, bruising, tenderness and itching at the injection points, which the reference page says generally settle within a day or two. Hypersensitivity to hyaluronic acid, bleeding disorders and active infection or inflammation at the site are listed among reasons treatment is deferred or avoided.[1]
Grokipedia lists per-session prices of roughly 300 to 600 pounds in the UK and 500 to 800 dollars in the US, with the caveat that its own ranges contain inconsistencies.[1]

Small open-label studies of roughly 11 to 64 participants report gains in hydration, elasticity and wrinkle scores lasting up to about six months, according to one source.[1] An expert panel consensus on stabilised HA skin boosters concluded that procedures of this type are minimally invasive, safe and effective for improving skin texture, and reviews of the category describe the evidence as varied in quality.[3][2]

A 2026 systematic review of nine studies and 278 participants of Profhilo and Profhilo Body reported statistically significant changes or trends toward improvement in viscoelasticity, elasticity, hydration, density and laxity at sites including the malar and submalar face, neck, inner arms, abdomen, hands and knees, and improvements in the Wrinkle Severity Rating Scale and Facial Volume Loss Scale.[5] Two of the review's five authors are affiliated with IBSA's Italian company, which is relevant context for readers weighing the findings.[5]

In Europe, Profhilo is sold as a CE-marked medical device. One reference page lists it on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods since April 2022 and states that it had not been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration as of January 2026, with US studies registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.[1][13]

In England, a separate legal change affects injectables in general: since 1 October 2021 it is an offence under the Botulinum Toxin and Cosmetic Fillers (Children) Act 2021 to administer a filler by injection for a cosmetic purpose to anyone under 18, with exemptions for approved medical professionals. Whether skin boosters fall under the definition of a filler is a question for the legal text, which is not discussed in the guidance reviewed.[14]

A worldwide post-marketing assessment of spontaneous reports from February 2015 to February 2018 covering more than 40,000 patients logged 12 adverse event reports, none serious; early injection-site reactions such as swelling, redness and bruising were most common, with two late-onset reactions such as nodules, and the authors noted that minor events may be underreported.[4] A 2025 update covering 2018 to 2023 estimated about 1.09 million patients exposed to the face product and reported 371 adverse events, a rate of 0.034 percent, most commonly edema, erythema and discomfort.[6]

HA injectables generally carry risks of bruising, nodules and, rarely, vascular occlusion.[15] The 2026 systematic review lists bruising, swelling, mild pinching, small bumps and localised hematomas, usually resolving within 72 hours.[5]

Registered Profhilo studies include a trial in malar and sub-malar volume deficiency (n=64), neck (n=25), inner arm and abdomen (n=24), back of the hands (n=51), and Profhilo Structura (n=164).[16][17][18][19][13] A 2024 single-arm pilot study evaluated intradermal HA as a skin quality booster.[20]

A 2024 split-face randomised trial in 12 patients with atrophic acne scars compared subcision alone with subcision plus Profhilo, assessing scars by sonographic depth, blinded photographic ratings and patient satisfaction, and reported higher patient satisfaction scores on the Profhilo side.[10] A 2026 triple-blind split-face trial in 12 women aged 45 to 65 compared Profhilo with saline in the perioral region, using stereophotogrammetry, ultrasound, photographs and a Face-Q questionnaire at 60 days.[21] In the neck rejuvenation trial, 19 participants per group were evaluated three months after treatment using the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale and skin biophysical measures.[9]

Profhilo is discussed mainly in clinic and aesthetics-press contexts rather than on looksmaxxing forums, where it appears as one option in the skin-quality tier alongside topical retinoids, microneedling and other injectables. Clinics commonly present it as an 'injectable moisturiser' for people who want better skin texture without visible filler. Grokipedia describes it as having become a staple of skin-rejuvenation protocols worldwide.[1]

lore.intro: Profhilo is described mainly by clinics, the manufacturer and the aesthetics literature rather than by looksmaxxing forums. Claims below are those made by practitioners and the product's proponents, set against what published research reports.[1][5]

claims.claim: It improves skin quality (hydration, elasticity, texture) without adding volume
The hybrid complex stimulates collagen and elastin
It is a safe, well-tolerated treatment
Results last about six months and can be maintained with repeat sessions
It can improve acne scars, necks, hands and body skin
Profhilo Structura restores facial fat volume

timeline.event: IBSA is founded in Lugano, Switzerland, by Swiss biologists.[1]
Profhilo launches in Europe with CE marking; a first registered study of the product in malar and sub-malar volume deficiency begins in March.[1][16]
A PLoS One laboratory paper on hybrid cooperative complexes is published (expression of concern issued April 2024).[7]
An expert panel consensus on stabilised non-animal HA skin boosters is published.[2]
Safety assessment of the high and low molecular weight hyaluronan product is published, drawing on post-marketing data from more than 40,000 patients.[4]
The Botulinum Toxin and Cosmetic Fillers (Children) Act 2021 takes effect in England on 1 October.[14]
Listed on the Australian ARTG in April per Grokipedia.[1]
Sisram Medical's China distribution agreement is announced per Grokipedia; Profhilo Structura initial clinical experience is published.[1][12]
Profhilo Structura practical review is published, and a registered Structura safety and efficacy study (n=164) begins in September.[13][11]
Update on nearly ten years of post-marketing surveillance is published.[6]
A systematic review of Profhilo and Profhilo Body (nine studies, 278 participants) is published.[5]
